concept.name: Cash-futures basis trade
concept.definition: The Treasury-market instantiation of the basis trade: arbitrageurs, chiefly hedge funds, buy cash Treasury notes and bonds and short Treasury futures when futures trade above their no-arbitrage price, financing the bond in the repo market so the position requires almost no net cash outlay. Profit comes from cash and futures prices converging by the delivery date.
concept.intuition: If the future is priced above what the deliverable bond plus financing costs, you can warehouse the bond, deliver into the future, and lock in the gap - as long as your repo funding survives until delivery.
concept.mechanics: Identify the cheapest-to-deliver Treasury, buy it, short the corresponding CBOT futures contract, and finance the bond with overnight or short-term repo while posting futures margin. The Office of Financial Research estimates hedge-fund basis positions peaked around $400-500 billion before March 2020, when margin and repo stress forced partial unwinds.
concept.formula: No-arbitrage condition: P(t,tau) = sum_s B(t,s) c_s + B(t,T) F(t,tau,T) - the cash bond price equals discounted coupons plus the discounted futures invoice price; violations define the tradeable disconnect.
concept.failure_modes: Overnight repo creates rollover risk and futures margin creates cash-call risk; in March 2020 rising margins and repo costs forced hedge funds to sell the cash leg into an illiquid market, amplifying Treasury-market stress until the Federal Reserve intervened.
concept.misconceptions: That the high leverage makes the trade speculative rather than arbitrage; the position is hedged against rate moves, and its fragility comes from funding structure, not directional exposure.
concept.example: From end-2017 to September 2019 hedge-fund Treasury exposure roughly doubled to $2.02 trillion while short futures positions rose $352 billion - the footprint of the long-basis build-up that partially unwound in March 2020 (OFR estimates).

citations.source: Barth & Kahn, 'Hedge Funds and the Treasury Cash-Futures Disconnect', OFR Working Paper 21-01
